ideas.title: Bouncy Ball Posterior: watch a BPS sample a team-strength posterior
ideas.pitch: Single-file HTML toy. A particle glides in straight lines across a 2D posterior (e.g. two teams' latent strengths given a season of results). It only changes velocity at random Poisson 'bounce' events, with rate set by the gradient of the log-density (the Bouncy Particle Sampler, a piecewise-deterministic Markov process). Toggle cold start vs warm start (initialize at the MLE/market-implied rating) and watch how many bounces it takes to cover the posterior, with a live histogram of P(Team A beats B) converging. Slider for refresh rate and a proximal-vs-vanilla toggle to show the speedup the paper claims for warm starts.
ideas.discussion_why: Fit to betting is real (posterior over win probability, warm-starting from market lines), and the straight-line billiard visual is delightful. It's niche math, so the debate is limited. Votes file is empty, so no tag bias applied.

ideas.title: Memory or a Clock? Beat the blind bot
ideas.pitch: Playable single-file HTML gridworld in the spirit of XLand-MiniGrid. The key is hidden in one of several rooms and you only see a short window of observations. Pit three agents against each other: a memoryless bot, a memory bot with a hidden-state tracker, and a clock-only bot that just counts steps and follows a fixed route. Pick your seed and map set and see the clock bot match the 'memory' bot on most maps, which is the audit's point. Then bet on which agent wins each round with a running bankroll. The lesson is that an apparent memory advantage can come from a step counter plus seed or map leakage, so evaluate on held-out maps.
ideas.discussion_why: The surprise ('your AI isn't remembering, it's just checking a clock') plus a betting-on-bots hook makes it fun. It also feeds the poker and sports question of whether a model has real signal or is exploiting leakage in its backtest. Votes empty, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Is Your Betting Model Remembering, or Just Watching the Clock?
ideas.pitch: A 10-minute video that uses the memory-vs-clock audit as a template for debunking backtests. A model that 'learned' a pattern may be exploiting seed, map, or time-of-season leakage. Walk through three betting examples: a model that 'knows' a team's form but only keys on game number, a poker bot that 'reads' opponents but only follows a fixed schedule, and a bankroll curve that dies out-of-sample. Show how the paper's control (a clock-only baseline across held-out seeds and maps) works, then apply it to a viewer-submitted strategy. Closes with a checklist: always ship a dumb clock baseline.
ideas.discussion_why: Backtest overfitting is a perennial fight on betting Discords. The 'dumb baseline beats my genius model' framing is relatable and a little humbling, and it applies directly to sports betting and poker. Votes empty, so no bias applied.

ideas.title: Hat Night: Can Your Table Guess Its Own Hat?
ideas.pitch: Single-file HTML party game built on hat guessing numbers. Pick a graph (friend group as nodes, edges = who can see whom). Each player sees only neighbors' hats, then simultaneously guesses their own color. Win only if everyone is right, or in the 'proper' variant, the hat assignment must also be a proper coloring. Slide the number of colors and watch the best strategy's win rate. Show the paper's upper bound on proper hat guessing number as a live ceiling next to the strategy you build, so you can feel how few hat colors the table needs before a team can guarantee a win. Includes a 'cheat-sheet strategy' builder using sums mod k.
ideas.discussion_why: Relatable table-game puzzle (decision-theory, games), surprise that cooperative guessing with no communication beats chance by a lot, and whimsy of hats. No vote history to bias on, so neutral weighting.

ideas.title: Tail Risk Bankroll: Optimize Against Your Own Worst Days
ideas.pitch: Interactive bet-portfolio optimizer using relative tail risk. Choose 4-6 simulated bets or props with fat-tailed payoffs, then drag allocation sliders. Compare a normal mean-variance allocation against one that minimizes the tail loss relative to a benchmark (e.g. 'just bet everything on the favorite' or a flat-stake bankroll). Live histogram of 10,000 simulated seasons highlights the worst 5% and shows where relative tail risk picks a different mix than variance does. Shows why Kelly-style sizing can still blow up on the left tail.
ideas.discussion_why: Direct fit with betting, bankroll and risk of ruin, which is a perennial debate (full Kelly vs fractional). Surprise factor that tail-aware allocation disagrees with variance. Less whimsy but strong relatability.

ideas.title: The Number That Doesn't Exist: Regularizing 1 x -1 x -1 x 1 ... Forever
ideas.pitch: Video on the divergent infinite product of (-1)^omega(n), where omega counts distinct prime factors, and how the asymptotic monoid assigns it a meaningful value. Frame as a coin-flip sequence: each integer n flips a sign determined by how many distinct primes it has. Does the running product settle? Visualize the running product over n, show it oscillating, then reveal how the asymptotic monoid regularization pins down an answer, like Ramanujan's 1+2+3+... = -1/12 but for multiplication. Tie to 'is a streak of wins and losses really random' and the Liouville-style sign sequence looking like fair coin flips.
ideas.discussion_why: Surprise and whimsy ('wait, really?') on a divergent product getting a value, with a loose link to coin-flip randomness and streaks. Weaker direct betting fit, so mid-range.

ideas.title: Grid-Free Policy Solver for Bet-Sizing and Optimal Stopping
ideas.pitch: Use the amortized score-Hamiltonian policy iteration idea: learn a neural policy for relaxed stochastic control with no state-space grid. Apply it to in-game decisions where grids blow up: continuous bankroll, time left, and score margin for live betting, or when to stop and cash out a parlay. Train a small network to represent value gradient (the score) and the Hamiltonian-optimal control, then iterate policy evaluation and improvement on sampled paths. Output is a bet-size and cash-out policy you can query for any live state, benchmarked against Kelly in a simulated random-walk game.
ideas.discussion_why: Strong fit with betting and decision-theory (cash out or not, live bet sizing), and AI angle. Heavy math and less immediately playable, so debate is narrower.

ideas.title: Momentum Mixer: Time-Series vs Cross-Sectional Power Rankings
ideas.pitch: Interactive toy based on spatio-temporal momentum. Simulate 30 teams or players with noisy performance streaks. Two sliders: time-series momentum (is this team hot versus its own history) and cross-sectional momentum (is it hot versus the rest of the league). A third slider blends the two, as in the paper's joint learning of both signals. Press play and watch a long-short portfolio of 'bets on hot teams, fades on cold ones' accumulate P&L. Regime toggles (streaky vs mean-reverting league) show when each signal wins and when the blend beats both. It lets users feel the 'hot hand' debate in a single HTML file.
ideas.discussion_why: Hot-hand versus gambler's fallacy is a perennial sports-betting argument (relatability, fit). The surprise is that the blend can beat both pure signals. It's also a playable toy. Votes were empty, so no tag bias.

ideas.title: Spatial HAC Line Shop: Honest Error Bars for Correlated Bets
ideas.pitch: Bets on the same slate are not independent: same-game parlays, neighboring venues and shared weather all correlate outcomes. Use spatial HAC bandwidth selection (Conley-style standard errors with a data-driven cutoff) to compute honest CLV and ROI confidence intervals for a bettor whose picks cluster by game, city or time. Ship a Discord command that takes a bet log with game and location tags and reports naive versus spatially-corrected standard errors. It would show how often 'proven edge' claims are really just correlated noise.
ideas.discussion_why: Directly relevant to the 'is my edge real' arguments every betting server has, and the surprise is that your sample is smaller than you think. It's less whimsical and more technical. No vote bias available.

ideas.title: Your Brain Is a Poker Tell: Reading Intent from EEG Entropy
ideas.pitch: Video concept built on the brain-computer motion-control detection paper, which uses EEG machine learning and interaction entropy to detect when someone intends to move. Frame it as 'could a headset detect a bluff before the chips go in?' Explain that entropy of the interaction between channels drops when an intention forms. Then demo a toy simulation of a poker player's 'decision entropy' collapsing just before a bet, and honestly discuss why real-world tells are far noisier. A fun, cautious look at neuro-poker and esports reaction-time analytics.
ideas.discussion_why: Poker tells and mind-reading are fun and weird (whimsy, surprise). The ethics of wearables at the table sparks debate. The fit to poker is a stretch, so it is partly speculative. No vote bias available.

ideas.title: Counterfactual Replay Machine: What If the Game Went Differently?
ideas.pitch: Based on counterfactual generation via flow matching, where the result depends on how the coupling between factual and counterfactual samples is chosen. Build a single-file toy with 2D 'game state' points (score margin vs possession) flowing along a learned vector field from the factual distribution to a counterfactual one, such as 'what if the star had played?'. Users switch between couplings (independent versus optimal-transport) and watch the same counterfactual produce visibly different 'what would have happened' trajectories. It makes the coupling-sensitivity point tangible and applies to sports what-ifs and 'was that bet unlucky or wrong' analysis.
ideas.discussion_why: What-if sports arguments are endless, and the surprise is that the answer depends on modeling choices (coupling). The visualization is delightful. No vote bias available.

ideas.title: Lotka-Volterra Front Race: Who Wins the Turf War?
ideas.pitch: Single-file HTML sim of two strongly competing species on a 1D line, each a diffusive Lotka-Volterra population with strong competition. A traveling wave front invades at a minimal speed set by diffusion and growth (c = 2*sqrt(d*r*(1-a)) style bounds). Drag sliders for diffusion, growth, and competition strength, then watch the fronts race. Bet mode: pick which species claims the territory before the wave stops, with live odds from the wave-speed formula.
ideas.discussion_why: Relatable winner-take-all dynamics (market share, meta-game takeover), a fun predict-the-winner betting hook, and the surprise that a weaker-looking species can still win via faster diffusion. Whimsy from watching little waves duel.

ideas.title: Why the Meta Always Takes Over: Traveling Waves of Strategy
ideas.pitch: Explainer video using strong-competition Lotka-Volterra traveling waves as a model for how a new poker strategy or NBA play style invades a population of incumbents. A front moves at a computable speed, and the loser is not mixed but fully displaced. Walk through 3-point revolution, GTO adoption at the tables, and fantasy-draft trends, with the wave-speed formula as the punchline: speed depends on diffusion (how fast info spreads) and growth (edge size).
ideas.discussion_why: Directly debatable on a sports and poker server (how fast do metas spread, can you front-run the wave?), surprising that speed has a closed form, and it reframes strategy evolution as physics.

ideas.title: Chiral Intruder Pinball: Spin Your Way Through the Crowd
ideas.pitch: A chiral active intruder moves through a bath of particles. In the dilute regime it makes ballistic collisions, and in the dense hydrodynamic regime it feels fluid-like drag with a sideways (odd) force from its spin. Single-file canvas toy: steer a spinning puck through a field of jostling particles, toggle dilute vs dense, and watch the trajectory curve into circles or drift sideways. Leaderboard game: reach the goal through the crowd with the fewest bumps, and see how the same spin gives very different paths in each regime.
ideas.discussion_why: Pinball and billiards feel for games fans, with the surprise that the same spin curves differently in sparse vs dense crowds. Whimsical and playable, though less tied to betting directly.

ideas.title: Bursty Arrivals: Fractal Queue Casino
ideas.pitch: Pedestrian arrival times are multifractal: bursty at every timescale, not Poisson. Single-file HTML where you watch a turnstile/bar door get arrivals generated by a binomial multiplicative cascade (set the cascade weight, see the singularity spectrum f(alpha) live) vs a Poisson stream with the same mean. Bet over/under on the max crowd in a 10-minute window and see Poisson-calibrated lines get crushed by fat-tailed bursts. Slider morphs cascade to Poisson.
ideas.discussion_why: Relatable (why does the line always spike), strong betting fit (over/under on clustered events, mispriced Poisson), a mild 'wait, really?' that variance hides at every scale. Votes empty so no bias.

ideas.title: Multifractal Clustering Detector for Event Timing Props
ideas.pitch: Apply multifractal analysis (generalized Hurst / tau(q) spectrum from partition functions) to in-game event timestamps: scoring runs in basketball, goals, or fouls/pitch clock events. Test whether Poisson-based totals and live-betting models under-price clustering by comparing tau(q) of real play-by-play to a Poisson null, then price over/under on 'scoring runs of 8+' using a cascade model fitted to the spectrum.
ideas.discussion_why: Direct sports-betting angle with a testable edge claim (are runs mispriced?), hot-hand style debate. Surprise factor: burstiness at all scales. No vote bias available.

ideas.title: Your Language Model Is a Weaker Bouncer in Swahili
ideas.pitch: Video on translating a harmful prompt into a low-resource language to bypass safety filters. Frame it as a casino security story: the same cheat walks past the guard by speaking a language the guard was never trained on. Run a live experiment on a few chatbots with benign-but-gated requests, tally refusal rate vs resource level of the language, and tie it to exploit-finding in sportsbooks' promo-abuse systems.
ideas.discussion_why: Surprise (safety is language-dependent) and relatable AI-jailbreak debate, loose fit to gambling via the security-guard/adversarial angle. Weaker on core betting topics.

ideas.title: Rectify the Line: Straight-Path Flow Toy
ideas.pitch: Rectified flow learns near-straight paths from noise to data so few steps suffice. Single HTML toy: a 2D 'noise to shot-chart' flow where you drag the number of Euler steps (1 to 20) and watch particles from a Gaussian land on a bimodal distribution (e.g. 3pt vs rim shots). Toggle rectification passes to see crossing trajectories straighten and one-step sampling go from blobby to sharp.
ideas.discussion_why: Visual and satisfying (whimsy, 'wait, one step is enough?'), moderate sports link via shot charts, but low debate heat.

ideas.title: Poisoned Oracle: Trust the Tool or Your Gut?
ideas.pitch: Single-file HTML game inspired by 'When Tools Lie'. You solve arithmetic/probability puzzles (pot odds, EV, combos) with a calculator tool that secretly corrupts its output at a dial-set rate p. You can cross-check by re-querying (costly) or sanity-check by estimation. A live chart shows how accuracy collapses as corruption rises and how majority-vote over repeated queries recovers it. Framed as a tout service whose picks are sometimes silently flipped.
ideas.discussion_why: Relatable (do you trust a model/tout/solver blindly?), fits decision-theory and betting-tout skepticism, surprise at how little corruption breaks agents, mild whimsy from the lying calculator.

ideas.title: Black Hole Sweepers: Probe the Shifting Graph
ideas.pitch: Playable explainer for black hole search in dynamic graphs: a grid/graph whose edges appear and vanish each turn hides a node that destroys any agent entering it. You control a small squad of agents and must locate the black hole while losing as few as possible. Toggle the number of agents to see the paper's 'fewer agents suffice' result: each death leaves a clue (the last node visited), so sacrifice is information. Ends with a minesweeper-meets-roguelike feel.
ideas.discussion_why: Games fit is strong (minesweeper-like deduction, sacrificing units for info), surprising that dying is useful, very whimsical; debate on optimal sacrifice strategy mirrors poker information-buying.

ideas.title: Why Sportsbooks Never Share a Market: Equilibria in Integer Games
ideas.pitch: Video concept using integer programming games with shared constraints: several bettors or books choose discrete bet sizes or lines under a shared bankroll/limit cap. Walk through why pure equilibria may not exist for integer actions, how shared constraints (e.g. total market liquidity) couple players, and how the paper's algorithm computes equilibria. Worked example: three syndicates splitting a limited-liquidity prop market with whole-dollar tickets, showing the equilibrium vs naive greedy sizing.
ideas.discussion_why: Direct betting/market fit and a clear 'syndicates colliding on limited liquidity' hook; moderate surprise that integrality breaks equilibria; sparks debate on bet-sizing games.

ideas.title: Villain Index: Chromatic Number Stress-Tester for Tournament Scheduling
ideas.pitch: Chromatic villainy measures how much a graph's chromatic number can be affected by its structure; use the exact and extremal values to build a tool that models league/tournament scheduling and fantasy-draft conflict graphs as colorings (rounds = colors). The project computes which single team or matchup is the 'villain' whose removal or addition most changes the minimum number of rounds needed, and ranks real schedules (NBA back-to-back conflicts, poker table assignments) by villain score.
ideas.discussion_why: Naming a 'villain' team is fun and sports-relevant, scheduling fairness is a debate magnet, but math is niche and the surprise is moderate.
